prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B042 to B024 alone. The first-round exchange did not weaken my scientific view that circuit QED opened a new regime, but it did change my judgement of what this committee can defend. B024 is a new measurement capability with a clear concept (the magic-wavelength lattice, which removes the trade-off between atom number and Doppler, recoil and Stark shifts) and a realisation that has been reproduced and surpassed by several independent laboratories, with clock-to-clock comparisons that agree. It has already made gravitational redshift visible over centimetres and sharpened bounds on drifting constants. The attribution to Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking it to record accuracy is the most compact credit on the shortlist. I also take seriously that four colleagues arrived at it independently from different fields and that Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson name it as their fallback; that is a scientific signal, not a head count. As a theorist who works next to experimentalists, I value that the systematics here are confronted with calculation (polarisabilities, blackbody shifts) and the agreement holds.
statement.case_against: The lineage question is not settled. The 2005 frequency comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems cover the tools, and nobody has yet laid the lattice-clock concept against the actual 2005 and 2012 citation texts. The priority and credit tail (SYRTE, PTB, NIST and others) and the 1e-18 figures rest on recollection, including mine, and should be checked against the record. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and I do not want the citation to lean on it, since that is an application. Finally, a two-name credit omits real contributors and Ye's share partly rests on record performance rather than the original idea. If the committee finds the lineage too close to 2005 and 2012, I would rather see B042 or B036 considered than a weaker pairing for its own sake.

responses.point: Kroll presents B024 as a clean case of progress limited by measurement precision, but asks whether it is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and discloses a distant link to the Hall lineage of Ye.
responses.response: I now share his view on the main point, and I think the distinction can be made in physics terms: the comb counts optical cycles and the ion clock controls one quantum system, whereas the lattice clock interrogates thousands of neutral atoms at once with the light shift cancelled. That is a different solution to a different limit (statistical resolution against systematics), and it gave a different kind of result, namely many-atom clocks at 1e-18. I would ask us to write the citation around that, not around lineage. His Hall-lab connection is distant and he has disclosed it; I do not think it affects the substance.

responses.point: Lindroth sees B036 as a strong second, rates B042 fifth over the Blais versus Girvin question, and notes that Ye's credit rests partly on record accuracy rather than the original idea.
responses.response: I agree that the Ye credit needs a clear sentence in the citation, and I think it can be justified: Ye's group demonstrated that the many-body lattice clock reaches and then sets the record accuracy and stability, which is what turned the concept into a measurement instrument others reproduced. On B042 I accept her ranking and concede that the Girvin problem is real; I do not want to carry a credit that I cannot defend. I also agree that the partition of Cirac and Zoller between B036 and B004 remains unresolved, which is why I keep B036 only as an alternative and not as a part.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, argues that B024 alone is the cleanest case and that adding B019 dilutes it, with the single Halzen credit as the weak point.
responses.response: On the question of a second part I side with him. I cannot add a second part just to fill the prize, and a superconducting-circuit or trapped-ion second part would be a poor fit with a metrology prize for different reasons: B042 because of my own conflict and the 2025 prize, B036 because of its unresolved overlap with B004. I defer to him and Danielsson on IceCube physics, but a one-name credit for a collaboration-scale discovery seems to me a real problem that the committee should not paper over. B024 alone is the configuration I can defend scientifically.

responses.point: Olsson supports B020 first, but says that if the credit cannot be shown to be exactly right, B024 is the better-documented alternative; she also says she would support my recusal on B042 attribution.
responses.response: I appreciate her honesty on credit, and I read her fallback as a real convergence point. I also accept her suggestion on B042: given my direct field overlap, I should not be deciding attribution there, and my move to B024 means I no longer advocate it. On B020 I remain outside my competence. What would make me comfortable with it in some future year is a more settled picture of the pairing mechanism and a credit that deals with Yuan Cao; at present those two reservations, which her own statement lists, are the reason I would not move it above B024.

responses.point: Eriksson argues for B020 as a prediction followed by an unexpected discovery, accepts that the field is eight years old and the mechanism debated, and keeps B024 as the honest alternative.
responses.response: I find his structure (quantitative theory first, surprising experiment second, reproduced widely) the right criterion, and B020 meets it. My concern is only with timing and credit, as he says himself, and I would not oppose B020 on science. Where I differ is that B024 satisfies the same test for robustness and reproducibility at present, with a cleaner credit, so if the committee has to choose one it should be B024. I note that he chaired the 2025 committee and has flagged care over B042; I agree that this should count against a second circuits prize this soon.

uncertainties: Whether the lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 citations; this has not been tested against their wording.

Whether the priority history and the 1e-18 performance figures, which come from recollection, survive a check against the published record, and whether SYRTE, PTB or NIST contributions change the credited names.

Whether to word the citation as an invention and realisation of the magic-wavelength lattice clock or as a discovery of new physics, and how much weight to give the pending redefinition of the second (I give it none).
If B024 fails, whether B042 with a Girvin-inclusive credit or B036 with a settled Cirac-Zoller partition would be defensible, and I should not be the one deciding B042.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work on superconducting circuits and circuit/waveguide QED, so my field overlaps directly with B042, and I am a Chalmers MC2 colleague of Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson. Chalmers hosted the 2025 laureates as WACQT guest researchers. I have withdrawn B042 from my preferred configuration and would accept recusal from deciding its attribution. I have no connection to Katori, Ye, or the Hall lineage. WACQT's interest in quantum technology is not affected by the B024 outcome, though I note that my first-round advocacy for B042 should be read with this in mind.
